title: DWARF — The Debugging Data Format
description: Take an address in a running program back to the file, line and local variable it came from, by reading the DWARF sections a compiler emits.
author: Underlayer
completion_criteria: Decode a .debug_line header and reproduce every row of a real line-number program, and explain how a debugger maps an address to a file and line.

modules.title: DIEs, Types, Scopes, Locations and Frames

concepts.title: Why DWARF Exists
concepts.description: The address-to-source problem, and what objdump gains from 115 bytes of .debug_line.

concepts.title: The .debug_* Sections
concepts.description: Six sections, who reads each, the SHF_MERGE flag, and what strip actually removes.

concepts.title: DWARF 2, 3, 4 and 5
concepts.description: What each version changed, and the two header layouts that silently break a reader.

concepts.title: The .debug_line Header
concepts.description: All twelve fixed fields of the v5 header, decoded from the real bytes of shape_v5.

concepts.title: Directory and File Tables
concepts.description: How a line number becomes a filename, in the two incompatible v2-4 and v5 encodings.

concepts.title: The Standard Opcodes
concepts.description: The twelve standard opcodes, the six registers they mutate, and the extended escape.

concepts.title: The Special Opcodes
concepts.description: The mixed-radix arithmetic that packs an address delta and a line delta into one byte, with every row of a real program worked out.

concepts.title: From Rows to Source Lines
concepts.description: Sequences, the two-rule address lookup, and the DW_AT_high_pc address-versus-length trap.

concepts.title: The DIE Tree
concepts.description: The tree at the heart of .debug_info: abbreviations, has-children, one unit per compilation, and the multi-table trap that fails silently.

concepts.title: Types and Type Chains
concepts.description: Following DW_AT_type through base types, typedefs, pointers, structs and arrays -- and the inclusive DW_AT_upper_bound that makes eight elements print as seven.

concepts.title: Scopes and Inlining
concepts.description: Nesting is scope: subprogram, formal_parameter, variable, lexical_block, and how DW_AT_abstract_origin lets one inlined function be described once and instantiated many times.

concepts.title: Location Expressions
concepts.description: The tiny stack machine behind every value a debugger prints for a local: fbreg, breg, the signed LEB128 operand, and the two different opcodes for the same idea.

concepts.title: Call Frame Information
concepts.description: The CFA, CIE and FDE, why a push is a one-byte rule change, and the three encoding traps that make .eh_frame silently undecodable.

concepts.title: Split DWARF
concepts.description: Skeleton units, the 8-byte dwo_id, and the str_offsets_base that lives in the executable and not the .dwo.

concepts.title: Finding Things Without Reading Everything
concepts.description: The aranges and pubnames indexes: what each answers, why the aranges tuple table starts at 16 and not 12, and why an index is never the authority.

concepts.title: Location Lists
concepts.description: The .debug_loclists table, the DW_LLE opcodes, DW_OP_piece across registers, and a disagreement between readelf and llvm-dwarfdump that only the byte offsets settle.

concepts.title: Range Lists
concepts.description: The .debug_rnglists table decoded walk by walk: three back-to-back lists in one section, two different opcode families, and why an address in a .o is a placeholder for a number.

concepts.title: Same Source, Different Target
concepts.description: One file built four ways. Which quantities actually vary with the target, which with the version, and why a 32-bit and a 64-bit unit can be byte-for-byte the same length.

concepts.title: Packages
concepts.description: The .dwp file and .debug_cu_index: how a debugger finds one unit among hundreds, and what the index is not.

concepts.title: DWARF 4 in Practice
concepts.description: The version before the version 5 restructure, compiled and decoded: the eleven-byte header, and the three sections that exist in version 5 and not here.

concepts.title: Type Units
concepts.description: The second kind of compilation unit: where it lives in DWARF 4 versus 5, and what the sixteen bytes labelled a type signature actually contain.

concepts.title: Call Sites
concepts.description: What a call that already returned looked like: the call-site tree, a tail call verified field by field against three instructions, and a computed argument.

concepts.title: The Other Unwind Section
concepts.description: .debug_frame decoded beside .eh_frame, and the one four-byte field where the two sections mean different things.

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a line program's rows say address 0x1129 is line 8, and 0x1137 is line 9. A lookup is asked for address 0x1134. Which row applies, and why is that not surprising?
exercise_decls.answer: The row at 0x1129, giving line 8 — because a row covers every byte from its address up to the next row's, so 0x1134 falls inside the line 8 range
exercise_decls.options: The row at 0x1129, giving line 8 — because a row covers every byte from its address up to the next row's, so 0x1134 falls inside the line 8 range|No row applies, so 0x1134 has no line information because it is not a row boundary|The row at 0x1137, giving line 9, because the lookup rounds up to the next row
exercise_decls.explanation: 0x1134 falls between 0x1129 and 0x1137, so the last row at or below it is the 0x1129 row, giving line 8. That is not surprising because a row is a range starting at its address, not a point - it applies until the next row begins. This is exactly why 0x113d, the add instruction, correctly reports line 9 via the 0x1137 row.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: The row at 0x1129, giving line 8 — because a row covers every byte from its address up to the next row's, so 0x1134 falls inside the line 8 range

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a call site records DW_AT_call_return_pc : 0x2a, DW_AT_call_origin : <0x2f>, and one DW_TAG_call_site_parameter with DW_AT_location = 55 and DW_AT_call_value = 73 7f. The DIE at <0x2f> is a DW_TAG_subprogram with DW_AT_declaration : 1 and no DW_AT_low_pc. What does 73 7f say, and was this a tail call?
exercise_decls.answer: The value is rbx - 1, and this was not a tail call. The 0x7f is a one-byte negative SLEB128, and no DW_AT_call_tail_call is present. The origin pointing at a declaration is the ordinary case, not the tail-call marker
exercise_decls.options: The value is rbx - 1, and this was not a tail call. The 0x7f is a one-byte negative SLEB128, and no DW_AT_call_tail_call is present. The origin pointing at a declaration is the ordinary case, not the tail-call marker|The value is rbx + 127, and it was a tail call, because the origin points at a subprogram DIE rather than a declaration|The value is rbx - 1, and it was a tail call, since DW_AT_call_origin names a subprogram that has no DW_AT_low_pc
exercise_decls.explanation: Two independent readings. The value decodes as DW_OP_breg3 with a single-byte SLEB128 operand 0x7f: the high bit is set so the value is complete, and bit 6 is set so it is negative, with magnitude 0x7f and 0x3f = 63, giving rbx - 1. Read unsigned it would be 127 and every call would report the wrong argument. The tail-call question is answered by the absence of DW_AT_call_tail_call, not by the origin: DW_AT_call_origin names the thing being called, and in main's case it pointed at a definition while here it points at a declaration, which is the ordinary case. Using the origin's contents to decide would misclassify this call as a tail call.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: The value is rbx - 1, and this was not a tail call. The 0x7f is a one-byte negative SLEB128, and no DW_AT_call_tail_call is present. The origin pointing at a declaration is the ordinary case, not the tail-call marker

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: you are walking the DIE tree, you have just read a DIE at 0xb4 that is DW_TAG_structure_type with the has-children flag set, and the next byte is 02. What does the 02 mean, and where does the next DIE go?
exercise_decls.answer: The 02 is the abbreviation code of the first child, and the reader has descended one level because the structure said it has children. It is the origin member
exercise_decls.options: The 02 is the abbreviation code of the first child, and the reader has descended one level because the structure said it has children. It is the origin member|The 02 is the tag number, so the next DIE is a DW_TAG_member at the same depth as the structure|The 02 is a DW_TAG_member at the same depth, because members are siblings of the struct they belong to
exercise_decls.explanation: Because the structure has children, the reader descends a level before reading the next DIE. That next byte is the abbreviation code for the first child, which in the reference binary is code 2, a DW_TAG_member named origin. The depth prefix in readelf's output changes from <1> to <2> at exactly this point, which is the visible sign that a level was opened.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: The 02 is the abbreviation code of the first child, and the reader has descended one level because the structure said it has children. It is the origin member

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a line-program row refers to file number 1. In shape_v5, which file is that, and what goes wrong if you answer with file number 1 read using DWARF 4 indexing rules?
exercise_decls.answer: It is /tmp/opencode/dwarf-research/shape.c — the second table entry. Using v4 indexing, 1 would mean the first entry, which happens to also be shape.c here, so the answer coincides while the rule is still wrong
exercise_decls.options: It is /tmp/opencode/dwarf-research/shape.c — the second table entry. Using v4 indexing, 1 would mean the first entry, which happens to also be shape.c here, so the answer coincides while the rule is still wrong|It is the first table entry, shape.c, and nothing goes wrong — both versions put the compilation unit's own file first|It is /usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/bits/types.h, because v4 file numbers start at 1 and types.h is the second entry
exercise_decls.explanation: In v5 the first table entry is number 0, so number 1 is the second entry — which here is also shape.c, so this particular lookup happens to still be right. But the reason it is right is luck, not design: v4 indexing maps 1 to the first entry, and on any real file with more than one source file the two rules disagree about every single name.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: It is /tmp/opencode/dwarf-research/shape.c — the second table entry. Using v4 indexing, 1 would mean the first entry, which happens to also be shape.c here, so the answer coincides while the rule is still wrong

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: your decoder reads an FDE from a .debug_frame section. The four bytes after the length field are 00 00 00 00, and the section's only CIE is at offset 0. The .eh_frame version of your decoder is being reused, which computes the CIE address as the field's own address plus its value. What does it compute, and what happens next?
exercise_decls.answer: It computes the FDE's own length field as the CIE. The CIE-id check then passes — because the value there is 0, which is the .eh_frame CIE marker — so the check ratifies the mistake instead of catching it, and the alignment factors end up being read out of pc_begin
exercise_decls.options: It computes the FDE's own length field as the CIE. The CIE-id check then passes — because the value there is 0, which is the .eh_frame CIE marker — so the check ratifies the mistake instead of catching it, and the alignment factors end up being read out of pc_begin|It computes 0, which is the CIE, so the decode succeeds and there is no problem in this particular file|It computes 0, which is the CIE, because .debug_frame also uses a pc-relative CIE reference and the value happens to be zero
exercise_decls.explanation: Both halves of this are the point. The correct reading is the value used directly: 0, which is the CIE at offset 0, and the decode succeeds. The pcrel reading gives field_address plus zero, which is the FDE's own length field. From there the reader takes the FDE's CIE_pointer as a CIE_id, and because that pointer is 0 it satisfies the .eh_frame CIE check, so the check that exists to catch this actively ratifies the mistake. The version byte then reads 0, which does not exist, so a reader that validates the version catches it and one that does not continues into the alignment factors, which come from the FDE's pc_begin and are therefore text-relative addresses. The resulting CFA is computed from garbage while every address it produces is a valid one.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: It computes the FDE's own length field as the CIE. The CIE-id check then passes — because the value there is 0, which is the .eh_frame CIE marker — so the check ratifies the mistake instead of catching it, and the alignment factors end up being read out of pc_begin

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: the CIE says DW_CFA_def_cfa reg=7 offset=8 and then an FDE says DW_CFA_def_cfa_offset 16. What has happened to the CFA, and what instruction in the machine code caused it?
exercise_decls.answer: The CFA moved from rsp + 8 to rsp + 16 because rsp itself dropped by 8. A push did it — the CFA is a fixed landmark and the stack pointer moves away from it
exercise_decls.options: The CFA moved from rsp + 8 to rsp + 16 because rsp itself dropped by 8. A push did it — the CFA is a fixed landmark and the stack pointer moves away from it|The CFA moved from rsp + 8 to rsp + 8 but the register changed to 16, so it is now the return address rather than the stack pointer|The CFA moved closer to rsp, from 8 bytes above it to 16, because a pop raised the stack pointer by 8
exercise_decls.explanation: def_cfa_offset replaces only the offset, keeping register 7, so the CFA becomes rsp + 16. A push is what moves rsp down by 8, so the distance from rsp to the fixed landmark grows by 8. This is the whole reason the CFA exists: it is a landmark that does not move while the frame pointer that measures to it does.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: The CFA moved from rsp + 8 to rsp + 16 because rsp itself dropped by 8. A push did it — the CFA is a fixed landmark and the stack pointer moves away from it

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a program runs correctly after you strip it. What does that tell you about whether the CPU reads the debug sections?
exercise_decls.answer: The CPU never reads them — they exist purely for tools, so removing them cannot change behaviour
exercise_decls.options: The CPU never reads them — they exist purely for tools, so removing them cannot change behaviour|The CPU reads them lazily, and stripping just makes the reads fail silently|The CPU reads them to decide which instructions are safe to speculatively execute
exercise_decls.explanation: The program still executes correctly, and that is the proof: execution never touched .debug_line or .debug_info. Only tools read them, which is why stripping is safe for production binaries.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: The CPU never reads them — they exist purely for tools, so removing them cannot change behaviour

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a reader has validated the version and consumed the fixed part of the header, so it is positioned at offset 0x0c. It reads header_length = 0x38. At which offset does the line program begin, and which two independent facts confirm the answer?
exercise_decls.answer: At 0x0c + 0x38 = 0x44 — confirmed by readelf logging its first statement at 0x44, and by byte 0x44 being 05 (set_column) with the next byte 23 = 35 matching the column readelf prints
exercise_decls.options: At 0x0c + 0x38 = 0x44 — confirmed by readelf logging its first statement at 0x44, and by byte 0x44 being 05 (set_column) with the next byte 23 = 35 matching the column readelf prints|At 0x0c, because header_length describes the fixed fields that end there|At 0x38, because header_length is measured from the start of the unit
exercise_decls.explanation: The reader is at 0x0c and must skip header_length bytes, so the program starts at 0x0c + 0x38 = 0x44. Two independent confirmations: readelf's first Line Number Statement is logged at [0x00000044], and byte 0x44 is 0x05 = DW_LNS_set_column which matches the 0x23 = 35 column readelf reports. The third check is that 0x44 plus the program length lands exactly on 0x73, the section size.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: At 0x0c + 0x38 = 0x44 — confirmed by readelf logging its first statement at 0x44, and by byte 0x44 being 05 (set_column) with the next byte 23 = 35 matching the column readelf prints

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a parameter's DW_AT_location is the two bytes 91 5c. Decode the operand and say what the expression computes.
exercise_decls.answer: DW_OP_fbreg with operand -36: the variable is at frame base minus 36. The 0x5c is signed, so it is -36 and not 92
exercise_decls.options: DW_OP_fbreg with operand -36: the variable is at frame base minus 36. The 0x5c is signed, so it is -36 and not 92|DW_OP_fbreg with operand +92, so the variable is 92 bytes above the frame base and is therefore a caller’s local|DW_OP_breg7 with operand -36: the variable is at rsp minus 36, since 0x91 is the register-relative form and register 7 is rsp
exercise_decls.explanation: 0x91 is DW_OP_fbreg, which pushes the frame base plus a signed operand. The operand is SLEB128, and 0x5c is a single-byte negative value equal to -36, not the unsigned 92. The expression ends with one value on the stack and no DW_OP_stack_value, so that value is the variable's address: frame base minus 36, which resolves to rsp + 8 - 36 at function entry.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: DW_OP_fbreg with operand -36: the variable is at frame base minus 36. The 0x5c is signed, so it is -36 and not 92

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a DW_AT_location attribute in the -O2 build reads 0x24 (loclist). What is stored at offset 0x24, and what does a debugger have to do to use it?
exercise_decls.answer: A table of address ranges and expressions. A debugger looks up the range containing the address it wants, takes that range's expression, and evaluates it. The first entry here is a zero-length range holding a DW_OP_piece pair, meaning an eight-byte value in two registers
exercise_decls.options: A table of address ranges and expressions. A debugger looks up the range containing the address it wants, takes that range's expression, and evaluates it. The first entry here is a zero-length range holding a DW_OP_piece pair, meaning an eight-byte value in two registers|The bytes of a location expression, and the debugger evaluates it directly as in the exprloc case|A base address, so that every later range in the section is relative to it|An entry in the section's address index table, which the reader dereferences to find the real range
exercise_decls.explanation: The loclist form means the value is an offset into .debug_loclists, not an expression. Offset 0x24 holds a list of offset_pair entries: the first is a zero-length range whose expression is DW_OP_reg5 followed by two DW_OP_piece 4 opcodes, describing an eight-byte value in two registers at one point in the code. To use it a debugger finds the entry whose half-open range contains the address being asked about, takes that entry's expression, and evaluates it. The form is the thing to check first: a reader that treats 0x24 as expression bytes goes to the wrong section and produces a plausible wrong value.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: A table of address ranges and expressions. A debugger looks up the range containing the address it wants, takes that range's expression, and evaluates it. The first entry here is a zero-length range holding a DW_OP_piece pair, meaning an eight-byte value in two registers

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a debugger stops at 0x1150 and wants the DIE for make_point. The .debug_aranges tuple says address 0x1149, length 0x80, debug_info_offset 0. Does that tell you where make_point is?
exercise_decls.answer: No — it says only that address 0x1150 is inside the compilation unit that begins at .debug_info offset 0. To find the DIE for make_point you need .debug_pubnames, which gives 0x15c
exercise_decls.options: No — it says only that address 0x1150 is inside the compilation unit that begins at .debug_info offset 0. To find the DIE for make_point you need .debug_pubnames, which gives 0x15c|Yes — the tuple points at the DIE for the function covering that address, so make_point is the DIE at .debug_info offset 0|Yes — because 0x1150 falls inside 0x1149 to 0x11c9, the function must be make_point, the only subprogram the aranges section knows about
exercise_decls.explanation: The aranges tuple answers a different question: which compilation unit covers this address, and it points at offset 0, the start of the first unit. It says nothing about which DIE is which function - that is what .debug_pubnames is for, and here it gives 0x15c. The two indexes are used in sequence, and each answers only the question it was built for.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: No — it says only that address 0x1150 is inside the compilation unit that begins at .debug_info offset 0. To find the DIE for make_point you need .debug_pubnames, which gives 0x15c

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a debugger has a skeleton unit from the executable. That unit carries a DW_AT_dwo_name and a DWO_id. A .dwp package exists and is loaded. What does the debugger do with the DWO_id, and what would it have to do differently if the package did not exist?
exercise_decls.answer: It looks the DWO_id up in the package's .debug_cu_index and jumps to the offset it names, opening one unit instead of scanning every .dwo file. Without a package it must open each .dwo and read every unit header until one matches — the same answer, found by brute force
exercise_decls.options: It looks the DWO_id up in the package's .debug_cu_index and jumps to the offset it names, opening one unit instead of scanning every .dwo file. Without a package it must open each .dwo and read every unit header until one matches — the same answer, found by brute force|It searches the index for the DWO_id of every unit, finds the one whose indexed name matches the symbol, and reads the function from that unit|It uses the DWO_id to verify that the .dwo file named by DW_AT_dwo_name is the right one, and skips the package unless the signature matches
exercise_decls.explanation: That is the entire purpose of the index. The DWO_id is the join key between the skeleton in the executable and the split unit in the package, and the index maps it to an offset, so the debugger reads one unit header instead of every unit in every file. The cost structure is what makes it worth a format: files read drops from all of them to one, and unit data parsed drops from all of it to a single header. The scan without a package is not incorrect, which is the subtle part: it is the same answer, arrived at by reading everything.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: It looks the DWO_id up in the package's .debug_cu_index and jumps to the offset it names, opening one unit instead of scanning every .dwo file. Without a package it must open each .dwo and read every unit header until one matches — the same answer, found by brute force

exercise_decls.question: Two compilation units come out of the same build system. One is from a 32-bit target with DWARF 5 and has unit_length = 165 with its first DIE at offset 0xc. The other is from a 64-bit target with DWARF 5 and also has unit_length = 165, first DIE at 0xc. Both use DW_FORM_addrx. A third unit is from a 64-bit target with DWARF 3, has unit_length = 263, first DIE at 0xb. What accounts for all three of those observations?
exercise_decls.answer: Three independent things: the indexed address forms mean address width never appears in the DIE tree, so the 32-bit and 64-bit units match; version 5 added unit_type to the header, making it 12 bytes instead of 11 and pushing the first DIE from 0xb to 0xc; and the much longer version 3 unit is content, because the older producer records a larger attribute set and stores some addresses inline
exercise_decls.options: Three independent things: the indexed address forms mean address width never appears in the DIE tree, so the 32-bit and 64-bit units match; version 5 added unit_type to the header, making it 12 bytes instead of 11 and pushing the first DIE from 0xb to 0xc; and the much longer version 3 unit is content, because the older producer records a larger attribute set and stores some addresses inline|The 32-bit target needs half as many bytes for every address, so its unit is shorter, and the version 3 unit is longer because the older forms store more data per DIE|The 32-bit unit is the same length because the smaller address size cancels the larger unit_type field, and the version 3 unit is longer because it has no indexed forms at all|The 32-bit target is more likely to be DWARF64, since fewer bits are available for offsets and the format widens to compensate
exercise_decls.explanation: Three separate effects, and none of them is the one most people expect. The identical lengths are the indexed forms: DW_FORM_addrx stores a small index rather than the address, so the target's address width never appears in the DIE tree at all. The 0xc versus 0xb first-DIE offset is the version 5 header's extra unit_type byte, eleven bytes before version 5 and twelve after. And the 263 versus 165 length is not the address width either: it is the content, because the version 2/3 build records a different and larger set of attributes, plus the older forms carry inline addresses. Address width, version, and content are three independent axes, and conflating any two of them produces a reader that is right about one configuration and wrong about all the others.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: Three independent things: the indexed address forms mean address width never appears in the DIE tree, so the 32-bit and 64-bit units match; version 5 added unit_type to the header, making it 12 bytes instead of 11 and pushing the first DIE from 0xb to 0xc; and the much longer version 3 unit is content, because the older producer records a larger attribute set and stores some addresses inline

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a DIE carries DW_AT_ranges: 0xc and no DW_AT_low_pc. The byte at offset 0xc in the section is 05. What does that one byte commit the reader to, and what would a reader get wrong if it assumed the following pairs were absolute addresses?
exercise_decls.answer: It is DW_RLE_base_address, so an eight-byte base address follows it and every later offset_pair is measured from that base. A reader treating the pairs as absolute would be wrong by the whole base address, and would place the code at address 0
exercise_decls.options: It is DW_RLE_base_address, so an eight-byte base address follows it and every later offset_pair is measured from that base. A reader treating the pairs as absolute would be wrong by the whole base address, and would place the code at address 0|It is DW_RLE_end_of_list, so the list is empty and the DIE describes no code at all|It is DW_RLE_base_addressx, so the following byte is an index into the section's address table|It is DW_RLE_start_length, so the following eight bytes are a start address and the next byte is a length
exercise_decls.explanation: 0x05 is DW_RLE_base_address, and it is followed by a full address_size-wide literal address, here eight zero bytes that relocations fill in. Because the opcode set the base explicitly, there is no low_pc to add, and every following offset_pair is relative to that base alone. A reader that treated the pairs as absolute would produce intervals starting at address 0 and 18 and 34, which is not merely off by a constant but off by the entire base address, and the resulting table would attribute code to no function at all.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: It is DW_RLE_base_address, so an eight-byte base address follows it and every later offset_pair is measured from that base. A reader treating the pairs as absolute would be wrong by the whole base address, and would place the code at address 0

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a DW_TAG_inlined_subroutine DIE has DW_AT_abstract_origin, DW_AT_call_line and DW_AT_ranges, and no low_pc/high_pc pair. What does each of those three attributes give a debugger, and what happens if a reader assumes the instance is one contiguous address range?
exercise_decls.answer: abstract_origin reaches the shared parameter and local descriptions, call_line gives the source call site to show the user, and ranges says the code is split across several address windows — so a reader testing a single range will lose the frame partway through
exercise_decls.options: abstract_origin reaches the shared parameter and local descriptions, call_line gives the source call site to show the user, and ranges says the code is split across several address windows — so a reader testing a single range will lose the frame partway through|abstract_origin gives the instance its own address range, call_line gives the parameter types, and the missing low_pc simply means the body was optimised away|call_line gives the machine address the body starts at, and the missing low_pc means the function was inlined more than once so no single start exists
exercise_decls.explanation: abstract_origin points at the shared DW_TAG_subprogram that carries the parameter and local descriptions; call_line says where in the source the call was written, which is what a user wants to see when stepping; ranges says the address coverage is fragmented. A reader that assumes one contiguous range tests pc against a single window and will fail to recognise the instance for part of the function, so its parameters and locals vanish from the frame view partway through.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: abstract_origin reaches the shared parameter and local descriptions, call_line gives the source call site to show the user, and ranges says the code is split across several address windows — so a reader testing a single range will lose the frame partway through

exercise_decls.question: Your release pipeline strips binaries to save space. Support keeps reporting crashes with ??? where the function name should be, but engineers can still see correct source file and line numbers. Which sections survived, and what single change fixes the rest?
exercise_decls.answer: The line table survived but the symbol table did not — strip removed .symtab — so ship the unstripped file to a symbol server and keep only the address-to-line data in the released binary
exercise_decls.options: The line table survived but the symbol table did not — strip removed .symtab — so ship the unstripped file to a symbol server and keep only the address-to-line data in the released binary|Nothing survived, so you need to re-run the build with debug info and symbols and replace the shipped binary entirely|The DWARF sections survived but .symtab was dropped, so re-adding symbols is the fix
exercise_decls.explanation: This is the signature of removing .symtab but keeping the line table. .debug_line and .debug_line_str are intact, which is why file and line resolve, but without .symtab nothing maps a raw address to a function name. Build with -s instead of strip, or keep a separate unstripped binary per release and upload it to your symbol server.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Apply It'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: The line table survived but the symbol table did not — strip removed .symtab — so ship the unstripped file to a symbol server and keep only the address-to-line data in the released binary

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: line_base = -5, line_range = 14. A special opcode's adjusted value is 3. What address delta and what line delta does it produce, and is the line delta legal?
exercise_decls.answer: Address delta 0, line delta -2 — and yes, it is legal: it is exactly how a loop's back edge is encoded, with the address moving forward while the line register returns to the top of the loop body
exercise_decls.options: Address delta 0, line delta -2 — and yes, it is legal: it is exactly how a loop's back edge is encoded, with the address moving forward while the line register returns to the top of the loop body|Address delta 0, line delta +9 — because the delta is line_base + 3 and the unsigned reading of 0xfb is 251|Address delta 3, line delta -2 — because operation_advance is the adjusted value itself when it is below line_range
exercise_decls.explanation: 3 / 14 = 0, so the address does not move. 3 % 14 = 3, and -5 + 3 = -2: a negative line delta. This is completely legal and it is how a loop's back edge is encoded - the address goes forward while the line register goes backwards, back to the top of the loop body.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: Address delta 0, line delta -2 — and yes, it is legal: it is exactly how a loop's back edge is encoded, with the address moving forward while the line register returns to the top of the loop body

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: you are decoding .debug_info.dwo on its own, with no skeleton file to hand, and DW_AT_producer comes back as unsigned int instead of the compiler version. What is wrong, and where does the value you need actually live?
exercise_decls.answer: The string indirection is indexed from DW_AT_str_offsets_base, which is 0x8 and lives on the skeleton unit, not in the .dwo. With base 0 every lookup is off by two entries, and a wrong-but-valid string comes back
exercise_decls.options: The string indirection is indexed from DW_AT_str_offsets_base, which is 0x8 and lives on the skeleton unit, not in the .dwo. With base 0 every lookup is off by two entries, and a wrong-but-valid string comes back|The .dwo does not contain the strings at all, so they have to be read from the executable’s own .debug_str, which is why the producer string is wrong|The dwo_id is the missing piece, because it identifies which string table to use. Without it the reader cannot tell the two compilations’ tables apart
exercise_decls.explanation: DW_FORM_strx is an index into .debug_str_offsets.dwo, and that table is addressed from a base recorded as DW_AT_str_offsets_base on the skeleton unit - value 8 here. Using base 0 shifts every lookup by two entries, so a valid string comes back as a different valid string. The base is deliberately not duplicated in the .dwo, which is why a reader with only the .dwo cannot get this right on its own.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: The string indirection is indexed from DW_AT_str_offsets_base, which is 0x8 and lives on the skeleton unit, not in the .dwo. With base 0 every lookup is off by two entries, and a wrong-but-valid string comes back

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: the program contains DW_LNS_advance_pc with the single argument byte 02, and minimum_instruction_length is 1. What address change does that opcode produce, and what would the same byte produce on a target where minimum_instruction_length is 4?
exercise_decls.answer: 2 bytes here (2 x 1), and 8 bytes on a target with a minimum instruction length of 4 — the argument is in units of min_inst_len, not raw bytes
exercise_decls.options: 2 bytes here (2 x 1), and 8 bytes on a target with a minimum instruction length of 4 — the argument is in units of min_inst_len, not raw bytes|2 bytes here, and still 2 bytes on any target, because the argument is always a raw byte count|2 bytes here, and 1 byte on a target with a minimum instruction length of 4, because 2 is divided by the minimum instruction length
exercise_decls.explanation: advance_pc multiplies its ULEB argument by minimum_instruction_length, so 2 x 1 = 2 bytes here. With min_inst_len = 4 the same byte means 8 bytes. The opcode is defined in units of the minimum instruction length precisely so the encoding stays valid when that length changes between targets.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: 2 bytes here (2 x 1), and 8 bytes on a target with a minimum instruction length of 4 — the argument is in units of min_inst_len, not raw bytes

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: the same type is compiled at DWARF 4 and at DWARF 5. readelf reports Signature: 0x697e73e0be025c89 for both units. The two sixteen-byte fields in the files are 89 5c 02 be e0 73 7e 69 1d 00 00 00 01 0c 00 00 and 89 5c 02 be e0 73 7e 69 23 00 00 00 01 1d 03 47, and the two Type Offset values are 0x1d and 0x23. What can you conclude, and what must you not conclude?
exercise_decls.answer: The signature is not sixteen opaque bytes. Its third 32-bit word is the unit's own type_offset in both files, its first eight bytes are version-stable and are all readelf prints, and only the fourth word is unexplained. So the two units have the same displayed signature but provably different full signatures
exercise_decls.options: The signature is not sixteen opaque bytes. Its third 32-bit word is the unit's own type_offset in both files, its first eight bytes are version-stable and are all readelf prints, and only the fourth word is unexplained. So the two units have the same displayed signature but provably different full signatures|The two type units are byte-identical, so a type signature is fully portable across DWARF versions and can safely be compared across tools and files|readelf is printing the last eight bytes, and those are the ones that differ, so the identical display is a coincidence of formatting and the signatures should be assumed different
exercise_decls.explanation: The signature decomposes cleanly and one word is plainly structural: u32[2] is 0x1d in one file and 0x23 in the other, which are exactly the two reported type offsets, so the third word is a copy of the header's own type_offset rather than hash material. Words 0 and 1 are byte-identical across versions, which is why readelf's 64-bit display matches. Word 3 differs and is the only part that is not already explained. So the field is part offset and part something opaque, readelf shows only the opaque-and-stable half, and the honest conclusion stops short of saying why. The trap this catches is treating the displayed 64-bit value as the whole signature: two units showing the same signature have not thereby been shown to be the same type.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: The signature is not sixteen opaque bytes. Its third 32-bit word is the unit's own type_offset in both files, its first eight bytes are version-stable and are all readelf prints, and only the fourth word is unexplained. So the two units have the same displayed signature but provably different full signatures

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a DW_TAG_subrange_type child of an array DIE carries DW_AT_upper_bound : 7, and the source said char label[8]. How many elements does the array have, and what would a reader that used the raw value print?
exercise_decls.answer: Eight elements, because the bound is inclusive and valid indices run 0 to 7. A reader using the raw value would print seven
exercise_decls.options: Eight elements, because the bound is inclusive and valid indices run 0 to 7. A reader using the raw value would print seven|Seven elements, because DW_AT_upper_bound is defined as the element count and the value 7 already says so|It depends on the element type — a char array of 8 and an int array of 8 would report different bounds
exercise_decls.explanation: DW_AT_upper_bound is an inclusive upper bound, so the valid index range is 0 to 7 and the count is 7 + 1 = 8, which matches the declaration. A reader that used the value directly would produce indices 0 to 6, printing seven elements and never reporting an error - the value is in range and the type is valid, which is exactly what makes this mistake expensive.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: Eight elements, because the bound is inclusive and valid indices run 0 to 7. A reader using the raw value would print seven

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: you are handed a compilation unit and told only that its version field reads 4. Its debug_abbrev_offset is 0 and its address_size is 8. Where do those two fields sit, how long is the header, and what is the offset of the first DIE?
exercise_decls.answer: debug_abbrev_offset at offset 6, address_size at offset 10, an eleven-byte header, first DIE at 0xb. The absent unit_type byte is the entire difference from version 5
exercise_decls.options: debug_abbrev_offset at offset 6, address_size at offset 10, an eleven-byte header, first DIE at 0xb. The absent unit_type byte is the entire difference from version 5|debug_abbrev_offset at offset 8, address_size at offset 7, a twelve-byte header, first DIE at 0xc. The layout is the same as version 5|debug_abbrev_offset at offset 4, address_size at offset 8, a nine-byte header, first DIE at 0x9. The header is the same in every version, so only the version field differs
exercise_decls.explanation: Version 4 has no unit_type field, so the layout is the older one: unit_length at 0, version at 4, debug_abbrev_offset at 6, address_size at 10, and the first DIE at 0xb. The header is eleven bytes, one shorter than version 5, and the whole difference is the absence of the single unit_type byte. Nothing in the file records the header length, so this is the case where a reader cannot infer its own layout and must be told by the version.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: debug_abbrev_offset at offset 6, address_size at offset 10, an eleven-byte header, first DIE at 0xb. The absent unit_type byte is the entire difference from version 5

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a v4 reader consumes a v5 file. At offset 0x06 the v5 file has 08 and the v4 reader expects the low byte of header_length. What wrong value does it compute, and where does its first incorrect byte come from?
exercise_decls.answer: It reads header_length = 3,670,024 and starts the line program at 0x380012, far past the end of a 0x73-byte section — its first wrong byte comes from v5 inserting two extra header bytes
exercise_decls.options: It reads header_length = 3,670,024 and starts the line program at 0x380012, far past the end of a 0x73-byte section — its first wrong byte comes from v5 inserting two extra header bytes|It reads header_length = 257 and starts the program at 0x10d, past the end of the section|It reads address_size = 94 and rejects the file, because 94 is not a valid pointer size
exercise_decls.explanation: v5 bytes 0x06-0x09 are 08 00 38 00, so a v4 reader computes 0x380008 = 3,670,024 and a program start of 0x380012, in a section of only 0x73 bytes. The root cause is the single added address_size/segment_selector_size pair in v5, which pushes header_length two bytes later and misaligns everything after it.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: It reads header_length = 3,670,024 and starts the line program at 0x380012, far past the end of a 0x73-byte section — its first wrong byte comes from v5 inserting two extra header bytes
